name: Najamba
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Heath, Jeffrey. 2017. A Grammar of Najamba (Dogon, Mali). Language Description Heritage Library / Deep Blue (University of Michigan), hdl:2027.42/139022, doi:10.17617/2.2397771. 455 pp. (Glottolog ref 302029 dates it 2014.)
catalog_locator: §2.1 Prosody, p. 9; §3.1.2 Embryonic metrical structure, p. 17; §3.1.3 Weight, p. 17
catalog_quote: Najamba is a tonal language. H is high tone, L is low tone. Syllables may be H, L, falling <HL>, rising <LH>, or bell-shaped <LHL>. All regular stems (nouns, verbs, adjectives, numerals) have a lexical tone melody with one (rarely two) H-tone element(s). Some stems have /H/ lexical tone melody, others have /LH/, /HL/, or /LHL/ melody, spread out over the relevant number of syllables, but none is lexically all-L toned. These lexical melodies are modified or overridden by tone overlays imposed by inflectional suffixes (verbs) or by syntactic constructions (nouns, adjectives, numerals). [p. 9] ... Najamba shows relatively little of the metrical patterning that pervades the phonology (especially the verb morphophonology) of the northern Dogon languages that I have studied, where the second syllable of CvCvCv... is subject to frequent vocalic reduction (to a high vowel or schwa, or to zero). ... However, “stem-final” is not a metrically defined position in the usual sense. [p. 17]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Najamba is a tone language with lexical tone melodies (/H/, /LH/, /HL/, /LHL/) on all stems and grammatical tone overlays; the grammar contains no statement of word stress at all, and its only metrical remark is that Najamba shows little metrical (syllable-reduction) patterning and that stem-final is not a metrically defined position.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Heath notes the light/heavy stem distinction is 'less important in Najamba than in some other Dogon languages' (§3.1.3, p. 17) and is a matter of tone-overlay mapping rather than weight.
new_statements.domain_note: Word/stem level lexical tone; tone overlays operate at word and phrase (tonosyntactic) level. No citation-form stress discussed. Hantgan et al. 2024 (Kindige variety) speculate in passing about iambic feet and a 'prominence clash' but make no stress claim.
new_statements.identity_note: Heath's grammar describes Najamba proper (villages Kubewel and Adia, in the valleys west of Douentza) and states (p. 2) that it 'does not describe Kindigué or Bondu varieties'; Najamba-Kindigué-Bondu is the whole dialect complex that Glottolog files under bond1248 (ISO dbu). Hantgan & Davis 2012, Green & Hantgan 2019 and Hantgan et al. 2024 describe the Kindige (Koira/Kolobinye) variety, which Heath treats as a dialect of the same language; Glottolog has no separate code for Kindige that I saw. The plateau 'Bondu' varieties (Borko, Dogani, Tintam) remain undescribed except for Kassambara 1987.

sources.locator: §2.1 Prosody, p. 9; and §3.1.2 Embryonic metrical structure, p. 17
sources.note: No word-stress statement anywhere. §2.1 Prosody (p. 9): 'Najamba is a tonal language' with H/L/HL/LH/LHL syllable tones and lexical melodies /H/, /LH/, /HL/, /LHL/, overridden by grammatical tone overlays. §3.1.2 'Embryonic metrical structure' (p. 17): Najamba shows little of the metrical patterning of northern Dogon; 'stem-final is not a metrically defined position'. §3.1.3 (p. 17): light/heavy stem distinction 'less important in Najamba'. The word 'stress' occurs only in an etymological aside ('originated as an unstressed there'); 'accent' only as a tone-mark term.
